imageCaption: Aaliyah standing in front of the gathered neighborhood at Riverside Park, her hand-drawn map visible, the white flowers from Mrs. Chen's bodega framing the scene. The afternoon light catches on the park's grass where Sully's center point still seems to glow softly.
text:
Telling people you're leaving is harder than Aaliyah had anticipated.

Not because they were angry. That would have been simpler. Anger could be argued with. Anger could be addressed with logic. But the neighborhood's response to "we're following the resonance frequency to Curaçao" was something else entirely—it was quiet. It was understanding. It was the specific kind of sadness that comes when you realize someone was always meant to be temporary.

The announcement had been scheduled for five PM at Riverside Park. The neighborhood had arrived by four-thirty.

"They know," Elijah whispered to Aaliyah as they stood near the tables, watching people settle into chairs with the careful movements of those preparing for something important. "Sully told me they know. He said their phones have been buzzing all morning with some kind of frequency that Mrs. Chen started spreading. Like a vibration that says 'something's changing.'"

"Sully didn't tell you that," Aaliyah said automatically. But she was watching Mrs. Chen, who was definitely organizing people in the same precise way she'd organized the tables, as though she'd anticipated exactly what was about to happen and had decided the neighborhood should face it together.

Anthony appeared beside his daughter with the license plate collection in his hands. The glowing had stopped, but the destination was now completely visible—Curaçao, unmistakably, showing through the pegboard like a promise. He set the collection down on the table where Aaliyah's map was displayed. The map that was about to become something public.

"You sure about this?" Anthony asked quietly. Not questioning the decision. Just asking if she was ready to say it aloud.

"No," Aaliyah said. "But the map's sure. The timeline's sure. And that's probably what matters."

Luisana moved to the center of the park—not commanding attention, just existing in the space where people were already looking. The neighborhood quieted. Sully, from his center point, lifted his head like he was ready to hold them all steady for whatever came next.

"Thank you for coming," Luisana began. She had her journal in her hands, and she was speaking with the careful precision of someone who'd been a journalist, who knew how to say true things. "Over the last ten days, our family has been mapping something that we didn't fully understand. We traveled through your neighborhood. We gathered your stories. We built tables and resonance points and something that looked like permanence."

She paused. Anthony moved to stand beside her. Elijah appeared on Luisana's other side—the family forming a unit, a statement.

"But the thing about the Cascade," Luisana continued, "is that it's not random. The glitches, the frequency, the stability that happens when families like ours move through spaces like this—it's all pointing somewhere. And that somewhere isn't here. Not because here isn't beautiful. Here is beautiful. You're beautiful. What we've built together is beautiful."

"But the timeline has a destination," Aaliyah said. She surprised herself by speaking. But the neighborhood was waiting, and someone had to say the specific hard thing. "The glitches respond to emotional resonance patterns. They respond to genuine connection. And the pattern we've been mapping shows that the strongest resonance point isn't the second Sunday. It's somewhere we're supposed to be next."

She stepped forward. She unrolled her map on one of the tables, the one nearest Mrs. Chen's most perfect white flowers. The neighborhood leaned in. They saw the concentric circles, the arc patterns, the northeast vector pointing toward a destination marked in careful hand-drawn letters.

"Curaçao," Marco read aloud. He said it like he'd been expecting this conclusion and was also deeply sad about it. "Your parents' somewhere."

"Our parents' unspoken dream," Aaliyah corrected gently. "And the timeline's final destination. The resonance route doesn't end here. It ends there. At a yellow-doored house near Willemstad, in a neighborhood that's waiting to become stable on its own while we move toward what comes next."

The park was very quiet. Not the uncomfortable quiet of rejection. The quiet of people processing that something they'd thought would stay was already leaving.

Mrs. Chen stepped forward. She studied Aaliyah's map with the precision of someone reading a document that mattered. Then she reached into her apron pocket and pulled out something Aaliyah had seen before—the blue morpho butterfly, sitting perfectly still in the palm of her hand.

"This appeared at the bodega this morning," Mrs. Chen said. "I found it on the doorstep. I've been carrying it because I knew." She paused. "I knew someone would need to see it. And I knew what it meant."

"Abuela Ida," Elijah whispered. He was looking at the butterfly like it might start moving again, might fly toward the northeast and mark the path one more time.

"Your grandmother," Mrs. Chen said, "came to my bodega once. Three years ago. She ordered flowers—blue ones, like Curaçao sky. She said her grandson was learning that the best things in life don't come from planning. She said he was going to teach his own family that someday. And she said when that teaching was done, when the family had understood what she'd tried to tell him, the journey would lead them home."

Anthony had gone very still. There was something working in his expression—gratitude and grief and understanding all at the same time.

"I've been keeping her memory in the bodega," Mrs. Chen continued. She held out the butterfly toward the family. "And now I'm giving it back. To guide you to wherever Ida knew you were supposed to be."

Luisana reached out and took the butterfly gently. It didn't disappear. It simply settled into her hand as though it had been waiting for her to be ready to hold it.

"When?" Marco asked. Not sad. Just practical. "When do you leave?"

"Tomorrow," Anthony said quietly. "We fly out tomorrow morning. We've already booked it—because apparently, the algorithm sometimes knows what we need before we do."

The neighborhood seemed to accept this. Not happily. Not without loss. But with the same kind of understanding that had allowed them to build tables that no one had scheduled, in a park that hadn't known it was ready to hold something beautiful.

"Then we'll finish the work tonight," Mrs. Chen said. She was already moving, already organizing. "One final Sunday dinner. Not for the glitches. For the goodbye."

Aaliyah looked at her map. She looked at her family. She looked at the neighborhood beginning to move with purpose—not planning, but flowing toward a moment that wasn't scheduled but was undoubtedly going to happen.

Tomorrow, they would leave.

But tonight, at Riverside Park, under the shadow of the butterfly that had marked their destination, they would feed the people who had taught them how to resonate.

One last time, before the frequency pointed them toward home.
